title: Classes and Objects
summary: Define classes with fields, constructors, and methods, create objects with new, and give them a toString.
intro: Every program so far has had one class, `Main`, holding all the code. A class can also be your own type that bundles related data with the methods that work on it. This lesson builds classes from fields up to constructors, methods, and `toString`, then shows what variables really hold when they point at objects.

steps.title: Fields and objects

example.title: Two dogs
example.prompt: Define a Dog class with name and age fields, create two dogs, set their fields, and print them.
example.output:
Before: null, 0
Rex is 3 years old
Bella is 5 years old
Total age: 8
example.explanation: `class Dog` declares two fields, so every `Dog` object carries its own `name` and `age`. Before anything is set, `rex.name` is `null` and `rex.age` is `0`, the default values. Setting `rex.age` never touches `bella.age` because each `new Dog()` makes a separate object. The total line reads one field from each dog.

practice.title: Two books
practice.prompt:
Define a Book class and create two books.

1. In `Book`, declare a `String title`, a `String author`, and an `int pages` field.
2. In `main`, create a book and print `New book: ` followed by its defaults in the form `title by author, N pages`.
3. Set that book to `Dune`, `Frank Herbert`, `412`.
4. Create a second book set to `Emma`, `Jane Austen`, `474`.
5. Print one line per book in the same form, then `Total pages: ` followed by the sum of both page counts.

Expected output:

```text
New book: null by null, 0 pages
Dune by Frank Herbert, 412 pages
Emma by Jane Austen, 474 pages
Total pages: 886
```

tests.output:
New book: null by null, 0 pages
Dune by Frank Herbert, 412 pages
Emma by Jane Austen, 474 pages
Total pages: 886

hints: Fields are plain declarations inside the class, with no value: `String title;`.
Print the first book before you assign anything to it so you see `null` and `0`.
Reuse one format string, `"%s by %s, %d pages%n"`, for every book line.

steps.title: Constructors and this

example.title: Three rectangles
example.prompt: Give a Rectangle class a constructor and create three rectangles in one line each.
example.output:
3 x 4, area 12
5 x 2, area 10
6 x 6, area 36
Total area: 58
example.explanation: Each `new Rectangle(w, h)` passes two arguments to the constructor, which copies them into the new object's fields with `this.width = width`. So every rectangle is fully set up the moment it exists. `main` then reads the fields with dot access to print each size and add up the areas.

practice.title: Three students
practice.prompt:
Give a Student class a constructor and create three students.

1. Add a constructor `Student(String name, int grade)` that stores both values with `this`.
2. In `main`, create Ana with 91, Ben with 85, and Cleo with 78, one line each.
3. Print each student as `name: grade`.
4. Print `Average grade: ` followed by the average of the three grades with 2 decimal places.

Expected output:

```text
Ana: 91
Ben: 85
Cleo: 78
Average grade: 84.67
```
hints: The constructor looks like `Student(String name, int grade) { ... }` with no return type.
Inside it, `this.name = name;` stores the parameter in the field.
Divide the sum by `3.0`, not `3`, so the average keeps its decimals.

steps.title: Instance methods and toString

example.title: Scaling a rectangle
example.prompt: Add area() and scale(factor) to Rectangle and a toString, then print it before and after scaling.
example.output:
Rectangle 3 x 4
Area: 12
After scale(2): Rectangle 6 x 8
Area: 48
After scale(0): Rectangle 6 x 8
example.explanation: `area()` reads the fields of whichever rectangle it is called on. `scale(2)` changes those fields, so the next `area()` sees the new size. `scale(0)` fails the `factor > 0` check and leaves the rectangle alone. `println(r)` and `"After scale(2): " + r` both call the overridden `toString`, so the object prints as readable text instead of `Rectangle@` and a hash.

practice.title: Bank account
practice.prompt:
Give a BankAccount deposit and withdraw methods and a toString.

1. Add `void deposit(int amount)` that adds `amount` to `balance`.
2. Add `void withdraw(int amount)` that subtracts `amount` only when it is not more than `balance`, otherwise it changes nothing.
3. Override `toString` to return `owner: $balance`, like `Maya: $100`.
4. In `main`, print the account, then deposit 50, withdraw 80, withdraw 200, and deposit 25, printing the account after each call.

Expected output:

```text
Maya: $100
Maya: $150
Maya: $70
Maya: $70
Maya: $95
```
hints: Inside a method, `balance` is this account's field, so `balance += amount;` updates it.
Write `@Override public String toString()` and build the text from the `owner` and `balance` fields with `+`.

steps.title: Objects are references
steps.body:
Objects live in a memory area called the **heap**. A variable of a class type does not hold the object itself. It holds a **reference**, which works like the object's address. Assigning copies the reference, not the object:

```java
Point a = new Point(1, 2);
Point b = a;            // b points to the same object
b.x = 10;
System.out.println(a);  // (10, 2)
```

Now `a` and `b` are **aliases**: a change through one is seen through the other, and `a == b` is `true` because `==` compares references. It is the same sharing you saw with `int[] b = a`.

A `List<Point>` holds references too. `points.get(1)` hands you the object inside the list, not a copy, so changing it changes what the list prints. For an independent object, build a new one: `new Point(a.x, a.y)`.

When nothing refers to an object anymore, for example after `a = null;` and `b = null;`, the **garbage collector** can reclaim its memory whenever it runs. You never delete objects yourself. Reassigning a variable (`b = new Point(0, 0);`) only points it somewhere else and never changes the old object.

example.title: Moving a point in a list
example.prompt: Store Point objects in a list, change one through a second variable, and print the list to show the alias saw the change.
example.explanation: The loop never copies a point: `rightmost = p` just stores another reference to an object already in the list. So `rightmost.move(0, 7)` changes that very object, and printing the list shows `(7, 10)`. `==` confirms both references point to one object. `copy` is a brand new object built from the same numbers, so moving it leaves the list untouched.

practice.title: Discounting the priciest item
practice.prompt:
Put three items in a list, find the most expensive, and show that an alias sees a price change.

1. Create a `List<Item>` holding Lamp 40, Desk 120, and Chair 75, in that order, and print `Before: ` followed by the list.
2. Loop over the list to find the item with the highest price, store it in a variable, and print `Most expensive: ` followed by it.
3. Call `discount(30)` on that variable, then print `After: ` followed by the list.
4. Print `Same object: ` followed by the result of comparing your variable with `items.get(1)` using `==`.
5. Build a copy with `new Item(...)` from the most expensive item's name and price, discount the copy by 10, and print `Copy: ` followed by the copy, `, list: `, and the list.

Expected output:

```text
Before: [Lamp $40, Desk $120, Chair $75]
Most expensive: Desk $120
After: [Lamp $40, Desk $90, Chair $75]
Same object: true
Copy: Desk $80, list: [Lamp $40, Desk $90, Chair $75]
```

tests.output:
Before: [Lamp $40, Desk $120, Chair $75]
Most expensive: Desk $120
After: [Lamp $40, Desk $90, Chair $75]
Same object: true
Copy: Desk $80, list: [Lamp $40, Desk $90, Chair $75]

hints: Start with `Item priciest = items.get(0);` and replace it whenever an item's price is higher.
`priciest` and `items.get(1)` hold the same reference, so discounting one shows up in the list.
The copy is a new object: `new Item(priciest.name, priciest.price)`.

recap:
- Declare extra classes after `Main` with no `public`. Fields are the data each object carries.
- `new ClassName()` creates an object. Read and write fields with `obj.field`.
- Unset fields start at `0`, `0.0`, `false`, or `null`.
- A constructor has the class's name and no return type. `this.field = field` stores a parameter in a field.
- Writing any constructor removes the free no-argument one.
- Instance methods use the object's fields. Some compute values, others change state.
- Override `toString` with `@Override public String toString()`. `println(obj)` and `"text" + obj` call it. Without it you get `ClassName@hash`.
- Variables hold references to objects on the heap. Assigning copies the reference, so aliases see every change.
- `==` on objects compares references. Build a new object when you need an independent copy.
- An object nothing refers to is garbage collected.
